args.text:
What's gotta be done before ya start the Car?

Start straight in with the radiator, before ya so much as touch the starter. Whip the cap off the top and fill her up with clean fresh water. Can't get water that's spotless? Then strain it through a bit of muslin or some other cloth like it, cos ya don't want any muck gettin' in and bungin' up those little tubes in the radiator. Fine as a hair, some of 'em. The whole system holds about three gallons (call it 11 litres). Now this bit's important, so listen up: don't run the car under its own steam till that water system's full. Not for a minute. Keep pourin' till yer dead sure the radiator and the cylinder water jackets are both chockers. How d'ya know? The water starts dribblin' out the overflow pipe onto the ground, and that's yer whole water system filled properly. For the first few days yer drivin' a brand-spankin'-new car, it's a beaut idea to check that radiator often and keep it topped up. Top the water up as often as ya find ya need to, no more fuss than that. And if ya can get rainwater clean, grab it: soft rainwater beats hard water every day of the week, cos hard water can carry alkalies and other salts that leave sediment behind, and before ya know it the radiator's clogged solid. (See chapter on Cooling System.)

What about Petrol?

Fill the ten-gallon (near enough 38-litre) petrol tank—nearly full, mind—and never let her run low. Now here's where ya don't muck about. When yer fillin' that tank, make sure there's no naked flame within several feet, cos the fumes are dead volatile and they get about quick, quicker than ya'd think. And never strike a match anywhere near where petrol's been spilt. The air for several feet all round is full of those fumes, and they're highly explosive, end of story. Keep the little vent hole in the petrol tank cap clear, cos if it gets bunged up the petrol won't flow properly to the carburettor, and then yer goin' nowhere. Need to drain the tank? Open the pet cock in the sediment bulb down the bottom.

How about the Oilin' System?

Soon as the car's yours, make sure she gets a feed of medium light, top-quality petrol engine oil, poured into the crank case through the breather pipe at the front of the engine (it's the one with the metal cap on it). Then down ya go, under the car, and in the flywheel casing (that's the tank that holds the oil) you'll find two pet cocks. Pour the oil in slowly, nice 'n easy, till it runs out the top cock. Leave that cock open till it stops runnin'—then shut it. Once the engine's been well and truly run in, she'll go best with the oil kept halfway between the two cocks—but whatever ya do, never, ever let it drop below the bottom cock. Every other part of the car's been oiled properly before it leaves the factory. Still, wouldn't hurt to check all the grease cups are full and the bits that need oil are gettin' it. (See Cut No. 18, also chapter on Lubrication.)

How are Spark and Throttle Levers used?

Right under the steerin' wheel ya've got two little levers, and they do all the talkin'. The right-hand one's the throttle: it decides how much mixture (petrol and air) goes into the engine. With the engine runnin', the further ya pull that lever down toward ya (they call it "openin' the throttle") the faster she goes and the more grunt she gives ya. The left-hand lever's the spark, and the spark's what sets off the petrol mix in the cylinders. Move that lever and ya "advance the spark." Bring it down a notch at a time, notch by notch, till the motor seems to hit its top speed. Push it past that point and you'll hear it straight off: a dull knock in the engine, like it's tellin' ya off. (See chapter on Ignition.)

Where should these levers be when startin' the Engine?

Usually ya want the spark lever in about the third or fourth notch of the quadrant (that's the notched half-circle the levers ride on), and the throttle opened about five or six notches. Bit of practice and you'll soon know where to set 'em to start her properly, no worries. But take care not to advance that spark lever too far, cos the engine can "back kick," and that's no joke.
